gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Notebookcheck measured the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at about 1,600 Wh usable (just under 79% of 2,048 Wh) on a steady 200 W load, against about 1,850 Wh at 1,800 W. That means a 2 kWh station gives up more of its rated energy at a light load like a fridge.
standout_why: I compared four cited rival pages. wattpowerstation.com already has CNET's measured fridge runtimes and self-use shares, gives 12 W self-draw for the C2000 Gen 2, says Elite 200 V2 self-use is 'not published', and cites Outdoor Life's 49–71% at 34 W for older units. homepowerfacts.com lists 1,600 Wh 'measured' for the C2000 Gen 2 but names no tester or load. theoutagebrief.com has only calculated runtimes at 85% efficiency. The Yahoo/CNET page returned 403, but ChatGPT's answer quotes its runtimes. So the 1,600 Wh figure is already out there without attribution. What's new is Notebookcheck as the named source, with the 200 W load, the side-by-side 79% vs 90% comparison and the date. The other named measurements I found (APH's heavy-load drain of the Elite 200 V2, Bob Vila's 30+ hours) either don't fit a fridge-sized load or are already on our page.
decides: It supports the current pick's caveat rather than changing the pick. Using Notebookcheck's light-load figure, 1,600 Wh on a fridge using 1.5 kWh/day (62.5 W average) works out to about 25.6 h before any extra self-draw. So 2 kWh units (C2000 Gen 2, Elite 200 V2, AC200L) clear 24 h only by a thin margin with an average or older fridge. That margin matches CNET's 26–29 h on a fridge averaging about 55–60 W. The finding backs naming a 3 kWh unit (BLUETTI Elite 300, Jackery HomePower 3000) as the pick for anyone who needs to be sure of 24 h. The 2 kWh class stays the value pick for an efficient fridge.

findings.label: Usable energy at a steady ~200 W load (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten)
findings.source_title: 11.6 kg lighter than its predecessor: Powerstation Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 review (Notebookcheck)
findings.note: Published 2026-02-24, updated 2026-10-05. The tester drained the unit with a continuous load of 'a good 200 W' and called it 'not a good value'. The test unit was the European version, which Notebookcheck says 'differs slightly from the US model'. Arithmetic: 1,600 Wh ÷ 62.5 W (a 1.5 kWh/day fridge) = 25.6 h; 1,600 Wh ÷ 50 W (1.2 kWh/day) = 32 h.

findings.label: Heater drain test (APH Networks)
findings.value: 2,028 Wh delivered in 2 h 1 min at ~987–1,006 W (97.8% of 2,073.6 Wh)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (Page 4 of 5), APH Networks
findings.note: Page 4 shows no author or date. The heater drew 987 W on the meter while the screen showed 1,006 W. My arithmetic: 987 W × 2.017 h ≈ 1,990 Wh and 1,006 W × 2.017 h ≈ 2,029 Wh, so the 2,028 Wh comes from the screen reading. This was a heavy load. It doesn't show what the unit delivers at a fridge's ~60 W average.
